title: Why Fireflies Glow But Never Get Hot ✨
description:
How do fireflies glow? Inside a firefly's tail, a chemical called luciferin reacts with the enzyme luciferase, energy and oxygen to make cold light, and the firefly blinks by using nitric oxide to switch the oxygen supply on and off.

Sources:
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-and-why-do-fireflies/
https://www.chemistryworld.com/news/news-in-brief/3002905.article
https://www.harvardmagazine.com/2002/07/no-on-a-summers-eve-html

script: Fireflies make cold light. Your old bulb wastes ninety percent as heat, so how do fireflies stay cool? Inside a firefly's tail, sits a glowing organ called the lantern. Its cells are packed with a fuel, luciferin, and an enzyme, luciferase. Add a spark of energy, and a puff of oxygen, and the fuel lights up. No fire, just chemistry. But how does it blink? The firefly controls the oxygen. A gas called nitric oxide opens the gate, air rushes in, flash! Close the gate, and it goes dark. And every flash is a message. There are over two thousand kinds of fireflies, and each one blinks its own code. Males flash as they fly, and females answer back. So, if you could flash one message in the dark, what would it say?
key_facts: Firefly light comes from luciferin oxidised by the enzyme luciferase, using ATP (energy) and oxygen, in the lantern organ at the end of the abdomen (Scientific American)

The light is 'cold': it gives off very little heat; an incandescent bulb loses about 90% of its energy as heat (commonly cited). Note: the old 'nearly 100% efficient' claim was revised to ~41% quantum yield in 2008 (Chemistry World), so the script avoids it
Flashing is controlled by the oxygen supply: nerve signals release nitric oxide, which lets oxygen reach the light cells (Trimmer et al. 2001; Harvard Magazine)
There are over 2,000 firefly species; many use species-specific flash patterns, males flash in flight and females answer from the ground (Scientific American)
